title: Custom Instrumentation for Chiroptical Spectroscopy
content: A 3D-printed sample fixture for the CD spectrometer, designed in Fusion 360, and the chiral metasurface signal it made reproducible. λ = 580–615 nm · visible Custom Instrumentation for Chiroptical Spectroscopy a fixed sample seat makes millidegree signals reproducible scroll to run the experiment ↓ Shadi Mirmohammadi, Tang Lab, University of UtahProblem: sample placementCircular dichroism (CD) measures the difference in absorption between left- and right-circularly polarized light. For a chiral metasurface, the signal is a few millidegrees riding on a much larger absorbance. At that scale, the position of the substrate in the beam matters. Hand-placing a coated fused-silica chip in the spectrometer’s sample compartment shifts and reshapes the spectrum from scan to scan, so successive measurements of the same sample are hard to compare.Fixture designI designed a two-part fixture in Fusion 360 and 3D-printed it. A rail mount slides into the Jasco spectrometer’s sample compartment at a fixed position along the beam path. A square substrate holder, with a recessed pocket and corner mounting holes, seats the chip at the same position and orientation every time. The holder took six design iterations. The two Fusion 360 parts (CAD preview renders): (a) the rail mount that fixes the position along the beam path; (b) the square substrate holder, v6, with a recessed pocket and mounting holes that make sample placement repeatable.Result: a reproducible bisignate CD signalWith the fixture in place, the diarylethene (DAE) chiral metasurface shows a bisignate CD couplet across ~580–61...

title: Electrochemical Sol-Gelation of CdS Quantum Dots
content: Growing 3D quantum-dot gel networks under applied potential: phase- and size-dependent electrogelation of CdS QDs. λ = 424 nm · violet-blue Electrochemical Sol-Gelation of CdS Quantum Dots sweeping the voltage turns free quantum dots into a network scroll to run the experiment ↓ Gels grown by applied voltage Zinc-blende CdS quantum dots assembling into a three-dimensional network at the electrode, at 1.8 V. Your browser does not support the video tag. 1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl · 36 µM CdS@TGA in methanol · gel nucleating on the Pt anodeShadi Mirmohammadi, Department of Chemistry, University of Utah, with the Luo lab; SAXS at the Utah Nanofab with Randy PolsonBackgroundColloidal quantum dots are tunable: their band gap and color follow their size. As isolated particles wrapped in insulating ligands, however, they are hard to wire into anything macroscopic. Gelation addresses this by cross-linking the dots into a continuous, porous 3D network that keeps quantum confinement while allowing electronic communication, with a large surface area for catalysis and sensing.Most QD gels are made by adding a chemical oxidant. This is simple, but it leaves residue and nucleation is uncontrolled. This project uses electrochemistry instead: anodic oxidation of surface thiolates forms S₂²⁻ bridges between particles, so the gel grows directly on the electrode. title: Photon Upconversion in CdSe–Anthracene Hybrids
content: CdSe nanoplatelet–anthracene hybrids that convert two green photons into one violet photon, and how the position of one carboxylic acid on the anthracene sets the upconversion yield. λ = 532 nm → 410 nm · upconversion Photon Upconversion in CdSe–Anthracene Hybrids two green photons in, one violet photon out scroll to run the experiment ↓ Seyedeh Shadi Mirmohammadi, Farwa Awan, Tsumugi Miyashita, Todd D. Krauss, and Ming Lee TangUniversity of Utah & University of RochesterPoster presented at the 2nd International Symposium on Photochemistry & Functional Interfaces (ISPF2), New York, 2024.View the poster (PDF). The 532 nm beam lights the table green, but the cuvette glows blue: anti-Stokes emission from triplet–triplet annihilation.Photon upconversionPhoton upconversion combines two low-energy photons into one higher-energy photon, here green in and violet out. A solar cell or photocatalyst can then use photons that would otherwise pass straight through, and bioimaging gains deep-penetrating excitation with a visible readout. The usual mechanism is triplet–triplet annihilation (TTA), which runs as a three-step relay: a light absorber, here a CdSe nanoplatelet, absorbs the 532 nm (2.34 eV) photons; a mediator covalently bound to the nanoplatelet surface accepts the triplet by Dexter transfer (TET1); a free emitter in solution, 9,10-diphenylanthracene (DPA), collects the triplet (TET2), and when two DPA triplets meet, TTA promotes one of them to the singlet state, which emits at 410 nm (3.06 eV).In the Tang lab, CdSe–anthracene hybrids built on this scheme are tuned ...

title: EIT-Like Terahertz Metasurface: a Full-Wave Design Study
content: A published EIT terahertz metasurface reproduced and extended in Ansys HFSS, covering metal thickness relative to the skin depth, substrate selection, and a coupled-resonator fit to the full-wave data. λ = 0.35 mm · 0.87 THz EIT-Like Terahertz Metasurface: a Full-Wave Design Study two coupled resonators open a window where light slows scroll to run the experiment ↓ Shadi Mirmohammadi, ECE 6310 (Advanced Electromagnetic Fields), University of Utah, Spring 2026 ·read the report (PDF)Coupled resonators and the transparency windowElectromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) is a quantum-optics effect with a metamaterial counterpart. When two bright resonators are coupled so that their responses interfere destructively, a narrow transparency window opens between two absorption dips, together with the steep phase dispersion that makes slow light and ultrasensitive sensing possible. Zhang et al. (Optics Express, 2022) built one at terahertz frequencies: an aluminum C-arc + S-arc pair on polyimide, with a transparency window at 0.87 THz and a peak group delay of 5.5 ps.I rebuilt that metasurface in Ansys HFSS and then asked two fabrication questions that the original paper did not address.Two fabrication questions The first is how thick the metal needs to be. At 1 THz the skin depth of aluminum is δs ≈ 84 nm, yet the paper deposits 200 nm, 2.4× more than needed for opacity. Since resonance quality saturates once the film exceeds δs, a thinner film may work identically while cutting deposition time and film stress. The second is whether polyimide is the right substrate. title: 10 kV β-Ga₂O₃ Photoconductive Switches
content: Impurity-engineered Fe:β-Ga₂O₃ photoconductive semiconductor switches that switch 10 kV with a near-infrared laser. λ = 808 nm · near-infrared 10 kV β-Ga₂O₃ Photoconductive Switches a laser closes a 10,000-volt switch scroll to run the experiment ↓ Hunter Ellis, Imteaz Rahaman, Afrouz Taherian, Seyedeh Shadi Mirmohammadi, Botong Li, Michael A. Scarpulla, Berardi Sensale-Rodriguez, and Kai FuDepartment of Electrical & Computer Engineering, University of UtahManuscript ready for submission (2026).Switching 10 kV with near-infrared lightPhotoconductive semiconductor switches (PCSSs) are optically triggered high-voltage switches. They are compact and fast, with almost no off-state leakage, and are of interest for pulsed-power systems, ultrawideband radar, and grid-scale power electronics. Ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductors such as β-Ga₂O₃ (Eg ≈ 4.8 eV) are ideal hosts because blocking voltage scales with critical field. The difficulty is that switching a UWBG material through band-to-band absorption requires deep-ultraviolet light, and high-power, fast UV sources are scarce.The workaround is impurity engineering. Fe doping introduces deep acceptor states ~0.8 eV below the conduction band of β-Ga₂O₃, so an ordinary 808 nm near-infrared laser can photoionize electrons from the Fe states into the conduction band. This sub-bandgap optical triggering keeps the material’s full high-voltage blocking capability. (The same Fe:β-Ga₂O₃ photoconductivity is used in my optically tunable THz metasurface, a very different device on the same material platform.) Transition-metal imp...

title: Excitation-Switchable Eu³⁺ Luminescence in GdScO₃
content: A nominally undoped crystal changes its emission color with the excitation wavelength, and its luminescence reports on substrate quality. λ = 236–270 nm in · 612 nm out Excitation-Switchable Eu³⁺ Luminescence in GdScO₃ tune the UV excitation and the emission color changes scroll to run the experiment ↓ Seyedeh Shadi Mirmohammadi, Afrouz Taherian, Yunshan Wang, Diego P. Fernandez, Michael A. Scarpulla, Steve Blair, and Berardi Sensale-RodriguezUniversity of UtahManuscript in preparation for Optical Materials Express (2026).Visible emission from a nominally undoped substrateGdScO₃ is a perovskite substrate used for growing epitaxial oxide films. It is chosen for its lattice match to titanates, not for its optical properties. The substrates we studied are commercial, nominally undoped single crystals from two vendors (Stonylab (100) and CrysTec (110)). Under deep-UV excitation they show bright, sharp visible emission.The emission comes from europium at the parts-per-million level, an unintentional trace impurity thousands of times below deliberate doping, roughly one Eu³⁺ ion per 10⁵–10⁶ Gd³⁺. Such a small trace emits strongly because of the host: the crystal is a dense lattice of optically active Gd³⁺, and energy absorbed anywhere in the Gd³⁺ sublattice migrates to the Eu³⁺ sites. The GdScO₃ perovskite structure: ScO₆ octahedra (blue) with Gd³⁺ (purple) between them. A trace Eu³⁺ ion (gold) substitutes on a Gd site (one per 10⁵–10⁶ Gd), and absorbed UV energy migrates through the Gd³⁺ sublattice to it.Emission color versus excitation wavelengthUsing the tunable deep-UV sou...

title: UV Photoresponsivity of GeO₂ Photodetectors
content: Measuring the deep-UV spectral response of ultrawide-bandgap GeO₂ detectors with a tunable third-harmonic laser source, in collaboration with the Fu and Blair labs. λ = 233–267 nm · deep ultraviolet UV Photoresponsivity of GeO₂ Photodetectors blind to sunlight, responsive to deep UV scroll to run the experiment ↓ Shadi Mirmohammadi, with Imteaz Rahaman, Botong Li, and Afrouz Taherian (Dr. Kai Fu’s lab) and Prof. Steve Blair, Electrical & Computer Engineering, University of UtahMotivationGermanium dioxide (GeO₂) is an emerging ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor. The film used here, rutile r-GeO₂(111) grown by MOCVD on r-TiO₂(111), has an optical bandgap of ~5.31 eV, deep in the solar-blind UV where sunlight does not reach the ground. This makes it a natural candidate for solar-blind UV photodetectors. Dr. Kai Fu’s group fabricated metal–semiconductor–metal detectors on their GeO₂ films (interdigitated contacts, 250 × 300 µm active area) and confirmed that they respond to a UV flashlight. The quantitative test is how the responsivity varies with wavelength across the band edge.Tunable deep-UV sourceTunable light at 230–280 nm is not available from a lamp. We generated it by third-harmonic generation (THG) of a tunable Ti:sapphire laser in Prof. Blair’s lab, using my setup for UV-pumped photoluminescence realigned for this experiment. Tuning the fundamental sweeps the third harmonic across ~233–280 nm, and I calibrated the power at each wavelength on a Thorlabs power meter with a UV extension.At each wavelength we recorded dual-sweep I–V curves from −10 to +10 V in the dar...

title: Optical Constants of 3D-Printable Glass on Doped SiC
content: Spectroscopic ellipsometry of Glassomer films on doped silicon carbide, with Cauchy and oscillator modeling of Ψ and Δ and validation against literature optical constants. Shadi Mirmohammadi, Electrical & Computer Engineering, University of UtahBackgroundDesigning a photonic device around a material requires its refractive index, the real part n and the loss k, across the wavelengths of interest. For a new or unusual material, no one has measured them yet. Spectroscopic ellipsometry measures the change in polarization on reflection, reported as the two angles Ψ and Δ, and the optical constants are recovered by fitting a physical model to them.This study measures Glassomer, a 3D-printable silica-nanopowder-filled composite that is debound and sintered into fused silica, on doped silicon carbide across 250–2000 nm at four angles of incidence.CalibrationBefore any measurement, the ellipsometer needs calibration against a known reference. The first choice was a bare doped SiC wafer, the same substrate already in hand. The instrument rejected it: “The error bar on the calibration parameter Ps is too large… Repeat the coarse and fine calibration procedures on a thin SiO₂/Si standard sample.”The reason is geometric, not chemical. A bare polished substrate sits near Δ ≈ 0°/180°, where the polarization state barely changes on reflection, so the calibration regression that solves for Ps becomes ill-conditioned and its error bar grows very large. The Woollam standard works because a thin thermal SiO₂ layer on silicon pushes Δ away from those degenerate values, so the regression...

title: Engineering Spin States in Si QD–Organic Hybrids
content: Time-resolved EPR shows that Si quantum dots transfer a fully spin-polarized triplet to covalently bound anthracene derivatives. {% include project-anim.liquid %}Mandefro Y. Teferi, Sanoop Mambully Somasundaran, Shadi Mirmohammadi, Ming Lee Tang, Jens Niklas, and Oleg G. PoluektovArgonne National Laboratory & Department of Chemistry, University of UtahPublished in Nano Letters (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03633Optical methods do not resolve spinQuantum dot–molecule hybrids are a promising platform for generating long-lived triplet excitons, which drive photon upconversion, photocatalysis, and singlet fission. Silicon QDs are attractive because they are nontoxic, earth-abundant, and can be covalently functionalized. Nearly everything known about triplet energy transfer (TET) in Si QD–molecule conjugates comes from optical measurements (photoluminescence and transient absorption), and optical measurements do not resolve spin. A photodetector cannot tell whether a triplet formed by spin–orbit intersystem crossing, by charge recombination, or by direct energy transfer.Time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance (TR-EPR) can tell the difference. This work is a TR-EPR study of triplet energy transfer in Si QD–organic hybrids.The conjugatesThe conjugates pair 2.65 nm dodecane-capped Si QDs with three anthracene derivatives, covalently bound through different bridges (~7 acceptors per QD): 9-ethylanthracene (9EA) through a flexible single bond, 9-vinylanthracene (9VA) through a π-conjugated C=C linker, and 9,10-bis(phenylethynyl)anthracene (BPEA), a larger and more ...

title: Optically Tunable THz Metasurface Absorber
content: An optically tunable terahertz metasurface absorber on Fe-doped β-Ga₂O₃: HFSS design, measured photoconductivity, the ITO electrode process, and the first resonator array on the crystal. Poster at IRMMW-THz 2026. {% include data-anim.liquid %}Seyedeh Shadi Mirmohammadi, Steve Blair, and Berardi Sensale-RodriguezDepartment of Electrical & Computer Engineering, University of UtahPoster at the 51st International Conference on Infrared, Millimeter, and Terahertz Waves (IRMMW-THz 2026), Salt Lake City: Monday, October 12, 2026, 17:30 to 19:00, Poster Session 1, Board 1. Poster (PDF). An earlier version was presented at the ASCENT Summer School on Semiconductor Science & Technology, University of Michigan, August 2026 (poster).AbstractWe present an optically tunable terahertz (THz) metasurface absorber based on Fe-doped β-Ga2O3, an ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor (Eg ≈ 4.8 eV). Despite this large bandgap, Fe acceptor states enable sub-bandgap photoexcitation at 808 nm, producing pump-power-dependent photoconductivity. Full-wave electromagnetic simulations for σ = 0 to 25 S/m show 82.2% absorption modulation and 95.0% reflected-power modulation at 300 GHz, establishing Fe:β-Ga2O3 as a promising platform for optically reconfigurable THz photonics.Introductionβ-Ga2O3 is an ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor of interest for power electronics and UV photonics. In Fe-doped β-Ga2O3, mid-gap Fe acceptor states lie approximately 0.85 eV below the conduction band.
